references.text: Fear fell upon the people—parallel to how fear seized all who witnessed Jesus' miracles.
The promise that the Lord would raise up a great prophet—the people recognize Jesus as the fulfillment of this promise when they say, 'A great prophet has been raised among us.'
Zechariah's hymn uses the same expression: 'The Lord, the God of Israel, has visited his people' (ἐπεσκέψατο), which the people repeat in Luke 7:16.
Zechariah prophesied that God would visit (ἐπισκέψεται) his people with salvation, and the people's outcry in 7:16 reflects this expectation.
The same reaction of fear and praise to God after one of Jesus' miracles: 'Fear seized them all, and they praised God.'
The Emmaus disciples refer to Jesus as 'a prophet, mighty in deed and word before God and all the people,' reflecting the people's confession in 7:16.
Elijah raised the widow's son at Zarephath—Jesus' raising of the widow's son at Nain is a clear parallel to this account, and the people's reaction points back to it.
Elisha raised the Shunammite's son—another Old Testament foreshadowing of Jesus' raising in Nain, showing that a great prophet has come.
The Pharisee Simon calls Jesus a prophet, reflecting the people's confession in 7:16 that a great prophet has been raised.
After the feeding miracle, the people confess: 'This is truly the prophet who is to come into the world'—the same kind of prophetic recognition as in Luke 7:16.
Fear came upon all who witnessed the apostles' signs and wonders—the same pattern of divine fear as in Luke 7:16.
When the people heard that the Lord had visited (פָּקַד) the children of Israel, they bowed down and worshiped—parallel to the expression that God has visited his people.
Ruth hears that the Lord has visited (פָּקַד) his people—the same theological theme of God visiting his people as in Luke 7:16.
